## Abstract

Proteins on the cell membrane cluster to respond to extracellular signals; for exam­ ple, adhesion proteins cluster to enhance extracellular matrix sensing. The matu­ ration of such receptor clusters may require additional adhesome proteins to adapt and reinforce extracellular signal sensing. However, it has been unclear whether the genes encoding these proteins share a spatial organization in the nucleus. Using the adhesome as an example, we show that subsets of genes that code for adhesome proteins exhibit relative spatial clustering and co-regulation in distinct locations within the nucleus. We use Hi-C maps and RNA-seq data from adherent cells to map the correspondence between adhesome gene localization and their expression. Inter­ estingly, we find that the genes encoding several transcription factors, cofactors, and chromatin regulators that regulate these genes are also co-localized with the

adhesome gene loci, thereby potentially suggesting a link between the extracellular matrix sensing machinery and gene expression. Additionally, we validate the spatial sub-clustering of adhesome gene loci using MERFISH data and DNA-FISH exper­ iments. Collectively, our results support an association between adhesome gene organization and regulatory state, with a possible role in cellular signal sensing.

## 1  Introduction

Cells must respond to various physical and biochemical signals in our tissues [1]. To achieve this, the plasma membrane of cells comprises several sensors includ­ ing receptors, ion channels, and others [2]. Using such sensors, cells can rapidly adapt to varying signals in the microenvironment via, e.g., cell matrix adhesion through integrin receptors [3], cell-cell interactions through E-cadherin receptors [4], or antigen binding through T-cell receptors [5]. A common underlying mechanism

For example, in the context of integrin-mediated mechanotransduction pathways [9], ­adhesion-induced RhoA signaling results in nuclear translocation of various transcrip­ tion factors, leading to the activation of genes coding for integrins and focal adhesion docking proteins [10,11]; adhesion-induced RhoA signaling also results in MRTF- A/B nuclear translocation, upregulating a set of genes necessary for stress fibers and mature adhesions [12,13]; FAK is another focal adhesion protein which shuttles between focal adhesions and the nucleus upon biomechanical stimulation, where it interacts with various transcription factors leading to changes in gene expression, including adhesion-related genes [14]. The feedback between focal adhesion matu­ ration and transcriptional output has also been studied in the context of cell motility and migration; the transcriptional co-activators YAP and TAZ mediate this feedback by modulating cytoskeletal and focal adhesion maturation to enable persistent cell motility [15]. We hypothesized that genes encoding adhesome components are spatially clustered and have similar regulatory profiles, and that loci encoding their transcriptional regulators are spatially proximal to adhesome target genes. We tested these predictions by comparing active adhesome genes with active non-adhesome genes in fibroblasts.

Recent progress in genomic and proteomic technologies have allowed the charac­ terization of various proteins involved in signal sensing and transduction [16–19] as well as measuring the spatial organization of genomes [20–23]. For example, many of the proteins involved in cell matrix sensing to assemble focal adhesions have been annotated. In addition, recent technological developments in genomics coupled with efforts in bioinformatics have resulted in the annotation of many of the transcription factors, cofactors and chromatin regulators that participate in regulating adhesome genes [24–26]. Furthermore, recent progress in chromosome conformation capture assays have allowed mapping the contact frequencies of the 3D organization of genomes in multiple cell types [21,27,28]. Additionally, fluorescence in situ hybrid­ ization (FISH) technologies have enabled the identification of the spatial location of particular genes and chromosomes in single cells [29,30], thereby validating the 3D organization of genomes obtained using chromosome conformation capture meth­ ods. Importantly, advances in sequencing methods have allowed to obtain not only high resolution maps of the spatial organization of the genome, but also the transcrip­ tional state of the whole genome [31,32]. Given the vast datasets that exist in the context of focal adhesion, we used adherent fibroblast cells to test this hypothesis.

Chromosomal conformation capture technologies provided early evidence for the spatial clustering of functionally related genes (located on different chromosomes). A data-driven study of the human lymphoblastoid cell line GM06990 revealed that genes belonging to the same functional group (e.g., genes that code for interacting proteins, participate in the same complex, or pathway) tend to colocalize in space [33]. More recently, interchromosomal genomic clusters that are both spatially colo­ calized and coregulated were identified in the IMR-90 cell line [34]. In this work, we investigate the spatial organization of genes encoding adhesome proteins and their regulators in the nucleus of IMR-90 cells. Using transcriptomic data, we first confirm that most adhesome genes are active in adherent cells. Using chromosome conformation capture data, we then show that the active adhesome genes are spatially clus­ tered in the cell nucleus as compared to other active non-adhesome genes. Interestingly, the adhesome genes also show strong transcriptional co-regulation. We then leverage transcription regulator binding data together with chromosome conformation capture data to show that the genes encoding transcriptional regulators of the adhesome genes are also strongly clustered with these genes. These different data modalities enable identifying tight clusters of adhesome genes and their transcriptional regulators, which we further validate using publicly available genome-wide FISH data, and DNA- FISH experiments on selected genes. These findings support an association between adhesome gene organization and regulatory state.

## 2  Materials and methods

### 2.1  Adhesome data

Adhesome data was retrieved from http://adhesome.org/, a literature-based protein-protein interaction network made of known interactions and cellular components constituting the focal adhesion complex in mammalian cells [43,44]. Study results for multiple mammalian cell types were used to construct this database, which is not specific to the IMR-90 cell line. The network includes 150 intrinsic components and 82 associated components, with a total of 6,542 interaction records (S1B Fig). The distinction between intrinsic and associated components is based on the location of the molecule: intrinsic components reside in the adhesion complex, while associated components transiently belong to the adhesion complex.

### 2.2  Regulatory data and processing

IMR-90 bulk mRNA-seq data [45] was retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under the accession number GSE16256 (sample GSM438363). Data from 47 cistromic marks were also obtained from ref [46]. who collected it from ENCODE [32], Roadmap Epigenomics [31], and the GEO, and released it on the TargetFinder GitHub page (link). In order to obtain the genomic profile for a gene, the number of peaks overlapping the gene’s location on the hg19 reference genome (obtained from ref [47].) was calculated for each feature using the Python pybedtools library. The profile vector of each gene was then divided by the gene length to account for the random incidence bias. For each feature, the feature matrix was then log(1 + 1000000x)-transformed, centered and standardized by computing the mean and standard deviation of the feature across all genes in the genome. To determine gene activity in GM12878, we also retrieved and processed as described above bulk RNA-seq data from the GEO under the accession number GSE90276 (hg19-aligned gene quantifications in log(1 + TPM) format from samples GSM2400247 and GSM2400248) as well as 100 regulatory marks from ref [46].. The likely category of histone ChIP-seq marks (active, repressive, unknown) was retrieved from ref [48]. and ref [49]., and the category of transcription factors and other protein ChIP-seq marks were inferred from protein function.

Gene activity was determined by hierarchical clustering with average linkage and Pearson correlation of the processed regulatory profiles; the two resulting clusters were annotated using RNA-seq expression and known active and repressive marks.

### 2.3  Hi-C data and processing

The Hi-C contact frequency matrices for IMR-90 and GM12878 from ref [28]. were obtained from the GEO (accession number GSE63525) at 250kb resolution and mapping quality MAPQ≥30. Intrachromosomal matrices were corrected for locus-specific bias using the Knight-Ruiz matrix balancing algorithm [50] using the Juicebox software (link). Interchro­ mosomal matrices were also corrected for locus-specific bias using a matrix balancing approach (see ref [28]. for more details). Namely, we ran the Knight-Ruiz matrix-balancing algorithm on the genome-wide contact matrix at resolution 250kb (GWKR normalization). Following normalization, centromeric regions retrieved from ref [51]. were filtered out in each interchromosomal Hi-C matrices, along with peri-centromeric regions within 2Mb of the centromere and outliers based on row and column sums (outside of the 1.5xIQR, where IQR denotes the interquartile range). Repeat regions from ref [51]., as well as regions already masked in ref [28]. were also removed from the analysis. The final Hi-C matrix was log(1 + x)-transformed. When we run the LAS algorithm, we further centerdize the final Hi-C matrix using the mean and standard deviation of contact values across the entire genome.

### 2.4  Topologically associating domains

We followed the steps outlined in ref [52]. to call TADs with the Arrowhead software [28] at a resolution of 5 kb, using a Knight-Ruiz (KR) normalization of intrachromosomal Hi-C maps. TAD search was limited to a sliding win­ dow of size 2,000 along the Hi-C matrix diagonal. In a subsequent processing step, we removed nested TADs and merged ­overlapping TADs. Overall, this process identified 4,443 TADs located on different chromosomes (except for chromosome 9), covering ∼35% of the genome. The resulting average TAD length is 225 kb, which is similar to the 250 kb Hi-C resolution used throughout this study. Illustrations and descriptive statistics of the TAD calling process can be found in S2 Fig. Diagnostic metrics [52] showed that the resulting TAD list outperformed TAD lists obtained using different resolutions (5 kb, 10 kb, 25 kb) or different Hi-C processing methods (KR normalization, no ­normalization). Computing the Measure of Concordance between these TAD lists revealed that normalization had a limited impact on TAD calling. Then, investigating the enrichment of CTCF, RAD21, and SMC3 (cohesin complex ­proteins) at the TAD boundaries showed that TAD partitions obtained at the 5 kb resolution exhibited the highest quality. Finally, ­enrichment of H3K36me3 (active mark) and H3K27me3 (repressive mark) in the TAD lists (measured as the log10-ratio between their ChIP-seq signals and compared with a null distribution derived from random permu­ tations) confirmed the high quality of TAD lists obtained at the 5 kb resolution. These diagnostic metrics are shown in S3 Fig.

### 2.5  DNA-MERFISH data

We retrieved DNA-MERFISH data from ref [30], where 1,041 genomic loci were simultaneously imaged in 5,400 IMR-90 cells across 5 biological replicates with a detection efficiency of ∼80% for each locus, yielding on average ∼ 1,700 probe loci detected in each cell. The probe loci used for DNA-MERFISH are ∼30 kb in size and cover the 22 autosomes and chromosome X approximately uniformly, with each chromosome containing 30–80 loci. The data is freely available on Zenodo. Maximum probe–probe distances were calculated for 3,668 cells with valid coordinate and identifier data. Subsequent removal of records with missing values across all columns, together with chromosome-X exclusion, retained 3,533 cells and 990 loci for downstream analysis. For this analysis, we considered loci and gene locations with respect to the hg38 reference genome; the gene location data was retrieved from the UCSC Genome Browser [47,51].

Probe loci were associated with active adhesome or adhesome TR genes within 500 kb upstream or downstream; sensitivity analyses used a 100-kb window or required direct gene overlap. To account for different cell sizes, probeprobe Euclidean distances in each cell were normalized by the maximum probe-probe distance in that cell (S4B Fig). The mean distance for each pair was computed over the cells in which both probes were observed (S4C Fig). For the

We used a two-sample test based on the number of nearest neighbor type co-incidences, as described in ref [55].. We created a 1-Nearest Neighbor graph among genes from both groups using the Euclidean distance to determine neighboring relationships. Then, we computed the number of edges between genes of the same group. We compared this statistic to a simulated null distribution where we com­ puted the same statistic under random permutation of gene labels, for 100 different permutations (see S6E Fig). We reported the one-sided p-value for that null distribution.

•	 Hypergeometric test: In Fig 3B, we plotted each TR of interest based on the percentage of genes it targets among

To identify important TRs, we adopted a null hypergeometric model for each TR, conditionally on the number of genes it targets among all active genes. For each TR, we computed the corresponding one-sided p-value. In Fig 3B, we also shaded in grey the area corresponding to non-significant TRs at the 0.05 significance level, after applying a Bonferroni correction to control the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER).

### 2.8  Large average submatrices (LAS) algorithm

The LAS algorithm [56] takes a real-valued data matrix X (of size m-by-n) as input and outputs contiguous submatrices U (of size k-by-ℓ) that have a high average, τ , when compared to independent standard Gaussian entries. Therefore, the Hi-C contact frequencies were log-transformed and standardized using the mean and standard deviation of the non-zero contact frequencies across the entire genome. The resulting distribution of non-zero transformed Hi-C contact values in the entire genome is reported in S7A Fig; we note that the LAS algorithm is robust to slight violations of the normality assumption.

We used a version of the LAS algorithm implemented in ref [34]., which specifically detects contiguous submatrices rather than arbitrary submatrices. A detailed description of the algorithm is provided in the Supplementary Information of ref [34].. In our work, the LAS algorithm search space was limited to contiguous submatrices of at most 2Mb-by-2Mb in size, i.e., 8-by-8 submatrices (at 250kb resolution). For each chromosome pair, each iteration of the search procedure was initialized at a random contiguous k-by-ℓ submatrix in the log-transformed and standardized interchromosomal Hi-C map, such that the initial submatrix contained at least one active adhesome gene or adhesome TR gene. There are 3,990,387,344 submatrices of size at most 8-by-8 in the collection of interchromosomal Hi-C maps corresponding to all pairs of autosomes. To control the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) of the procedure at 0.0001, we used a Bonferroni correction and identified submatrices whose LAS p-value was below 0.0001/3,990,387,344 = 2.5 · 10–14. To be even more conservative, we applied a p-value cutoff of 10–15, as shown in S7B Fig.

The resulting distribution of average Hi-C contacts of the submatrices selected by the LAS algorithm is displayed in S7C Fig, where we also show a Hi-C cutoff at 2 (dashed red vertical line). We used this threshold to discard submatrices detected by LAS whose average Hi-C contact value was low. For example, the LAS submatrices identified for the chro­ mosome pair 19–20 before and after applying the Hi-C threshold are reported in S7D–S7E Fig. Thresholding based on the average Hi-C value alone is slightly different from thresholding based on the p-value, because the p-value depends on both the average Hi-C value and the dimension of the submatrix.

### 2.13  Image analysis

The nuclear mask was obtained via nuclear segmentation using multi-thresholding. The adhesome gene loci were seg­ mented using the intensity and volume-based threshold. For intensity based threshold, pixels with intensity more than Th were first binarized; here Th is given by the expression: Th = µ(I) + σ(I), where µ(I) is the voxel-wise mean and σ(I) is the voxel-wise standard deviation of the intensity distribution of IAdhsomeFISH, IControlFISH, and IRNAPOL2 in the segmented nuclei regions. For volume based threshold, gene loci were identified to be the distinct segmented regions with volume greater than 0.5 µm3. The pairwise distance was calculated on the centroid of gene loci. The dilated mask of adhesome gene loci was obtained by using slice-wise dilation using a disk element of 8 pixels. The pRNA Pol2 intensity was evaluated on the dilated mask of adhesome gene loci. All the image analysis was done using the open-source Python scikit-image [60] library. We computed a centric radial distribution function (RDF) by using the geometric center of the nuclear binary mask bounding box as the reference point. For each segmented object, the distance from its centroid to this center was calcu­ lated and binned into concentric annuli of equal radial width. The number of objects in each annulus was normalized by the annular area and the mean particle density, such that centric radial distribution function = 1 corresponds to a uniform spatial distribution. Similarly, we evaluated the particle radial distribution function (PRDF) using computed all pairwise distances between their centroids. Distances were grouped into radial bins of equal width, and the counts in each bin were normalized by the annular area and the expected number of neighbors based on the global object density. Under a spatially uniform (Poisson) distribution, this normalization yields PRDF = 1, whereas deviations from 1 indicate spatial clustering (PRDF > 1) or depletion (PRDF < 1) at the corresponding distance scales.

## 3  Results

3.1  Genes coding for focal adhesion proteins that are clustered on the cell membrane show strong spatial clustering in the cell nucleus

We sought to analyze the proximity of adhesome genes in an adherent cell type, using IMR-90, a human female fetal lung fibroblast cell line as a model system. As a first step, we obtained a curated list of 232 proteins that reside directly or indi­ rectly in adhesion sites from different cell types [43]. These proteins include integrins, actin regulators, adaptor proteins that link the cytoskeletal structures to the cytoplasmic tails of integrins, as well as a variety of signaling molecules (S8 Fig, S1 File). Gene set enrichment analysis confirmed the key role of these genes in regulating cell-matrix adhesion, migra­ tion, and cytoskeletal organization, among others (S1A Fig). A number of studies have shown that adhesome proteins are densely linked via binding or signaling interactions, suggesting that these proteins have to work together in the adhesome

Next, we analyzed expression data of adherent cells to verify that the adhesome genes are actively being transcribed. For this, we retrieved from previous studies bulk RNA-seq data [45], as well as preprocessed data on 47 cistromic marks [46] for IMR-90 cells. The regulatory marks included chromatin accessibility data (DNase-seq) and a selection of his­ tone and transcription proteins ChIP-seq data, among others (S10A Fig). This data was collectively used to determine the activity status of genes in IMR-90. In particular, we identified regulatory signals corresponding to 25,959 genes, whose genomic locations were obtained from a previous study [47]. We applied hierarchical clustering with average linkage to this data to identify two clusters of genes, cluster 1 containing 14,122 genes and cluster 2 containing 11,837 genes (S10B Fig and Methods). These two clusters are depicted in the t-distributed Stochastic Neighborhood Embed­ ding (t-SNE) plot of Fig 1A. By comparing the activity status of each of the two gene clusters based on the distribution of RNA-seq expression, we identified cluster 1 to correspond to active genes and cluster 2 to correspond to inactive genes (Fig 1B); the difference in expression is highly significant (Wilcoxon rank-sums test, p-value≤ 3 · 10–308) and consistent with peaks from known active marks (e.g., POLR2A, H3K36me3) and repressive marks (e.g., H3K9me3, H3K27me3).

Of the 232 curated adhesome components, 222 genes could be matched to the autosomal hg19 gene annotation used for downstream analysis [47,51]. Of these, 202 genes were found to be active in IMR-90 cells. These active adhesome genes are represented as light green dots in the t-SNE plot of Fig 1A. This representation was obtained using available transcriptomic data as well as data on 1D genomic marks (due to limited public data availability, noncoding RNAs, which are known to play a role in chromatin tethering [38,61], could not be considered in this analysis). For comparison, conduct­ ing a similar analysis in GM12878, a human lymphoblastoid cell line, showed that only 172 adhesome genes were iden­ tified as active in this non-adherent cell line (S11 Fig). While, as expected, this number is lower compared to IMR-90, a good proportion of adhesome genes remain active in GM12878 as they participate in other signaling pathways in this cell type. For example, the B cell receptor (BCR) signaling pathway is mostly active in GM12878, which is a ­B-lymphoblastoid cell line (63 BCR genes are active out of 81 in our data); this pathway is related to other signaling pathways [62–64] including actin cytoskeleton organization, MAPK signaling, NF-κB signaling and calcium-mediated signaling, which con­ tain genes that overlap with active adhesome genes in GM12878 (S12 Fig).

The identified adhesome genes are distributed on all 22 autosomes (Fig 1C), suggesting that interchromosomal inter­ actions may be essential for their co-regulation. 3.3  Transcription regulators targeting adhesome genes in IMR-90 cells are co-clustered with active adhesome genes

Because transcription factors, cofactors, and chromatin regulators (collectively abbreviated as TRs) play a key role in the regulation and homeostasis of gene expression programs, we next sought to identify the TRs involved in the expres­ sion of active adhesome genes in IMR-90 cells. We retrieved data on 5,896,536 TR-target relationships corresponding to 333 TRs and 55,714 target genes in several tissues from hTFtarget [24], a curated database constructed from largescale ChIP-seq data of human TRs in many conditions, as well as predicted interactions via TR binding site scanning. Among this data, we selected TR-target links present in several normal human lung fibroblast cell lines or samples from tissues, including IMR-90, WI38, AG04450, HPF and NHLF. While the majority of the TR-target data stems from IMR- 90 (S17A Fig), also considering the other human lung fibroblast cell lines provided additional TR-target relationships (S17B Fig), as well as four additional TRs (SUMO1, SUMO2, UBE2I and PIAS4) which are present in the WI38 TR-target data yet absent from the IMR-90 data, but active in IMR-90 cells (S17C–S17D Fig). All 31 TRs are shown as magenta dots on the tSNE plot of S18A Fig, along with the adhesome genes (light green dots). We observed that 28 out of the 31 TRs present in these cell lines in hTFtarget are active in IMR-90 according to our regulatory analysis (CHD1, SNAPC4 and SPI1 were discarded as inactive). Among these 28 TRs, 26 target at least one active adhesome gene (SNAPC1 and SNAPC5 only target inactive adhesome genes). In the remainder of this paper, we use “adhesome TR” to refer to a TR (or the gene that codes for this TR) that targets at least one active adhesome gene.

There is heterogeneity in the overall number of active genes targeted by these TRs, with some TRs targeting less than 50 active genes (UBE2I, SNAPC1, SNAPC2, SNAPC4) and other TRs targeting more than 10,000 active genes (LMNB1, MAZ, POLR2A); see Fig 3A. This heterogeneity may reflect both the specificity of a given TR as well as potential missing data from hTFtarget. Interestingly, active adhesome genes tend to be more targeted by the identified TRs than similar random active non-adhesome genes (Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test, p-value≤ 2 · 10–10; see S19A Fig), supporting the potential role of the identified TRs in adhesome regulation. Conditional on their total number of active gene targets, we identified 13 TRs whose target genes contained adhesome genes at a significantly higher proportion than expected under a hypergeometric test (family-wise error rate control, FWER, at 5% with Bonferroni correction). These 13 TRs lie outside of the shaded 5% Bonferroni-corrected hypergeometric confidence region in Fig 3B. These include TRs that have been identified to play a role in adhesion in previous research: LMNB1 plays an important role in cellular response to mechanical stress [68], RAD21 regulates the cadherin and cell adhesion pathway [69], and EP300 actively controls cell adhesion [70], among others. The regulators POLR2A, CTCF, MAZ, CEBPB and LMNB1 have the smallest FWER-adjusted p-values and target more than 80% of active adhesome genes, suggesting a high level of redundancy and co-regulation (Fig 3C).

The 13 significant adhesome TR genes correspond to 15 distinct 250 kb genomic loci, and the 13 remaining adhe­ some TR genes correspond to 14 distinct genomic loci. 3.4  Clustering analysis identifies interactions of closely localized and co-regulated adhesome genes and their transcription regulators

Seeded in active adhesome loci, the LAS algorithm greedily identifies contiguous submatrices in which the average contact frequency is significantly higher than expected by chance (see Methods). ## 4  Discussion

Cells have evolved to organize their receptors on the plasma membrane for signal sensing [1–6]. In addition, the genetic material is packed within the cell nucleus to encode the various cellular proteins [20–23]. In recent years two aspects of spatial clustering have been identified, one at the level of receptors for optimized signal sensing, and the other at the level of genes for optimized transcriptional regulation. While these two layers of clustering may appear independent of each other, we hypothesized that there may exist a coupling between the two spaces. The main premise of this hypothesis is due to cells having to detect the extracellular signals through their receptors and needing to transcriptionally reinforce the sensing machinery for rapid adaptation [71]. Spatial clustering of the corresponding genes could contribute to their coordi­ nated regulation; a role in rapid cellular response remains to be tested.

To test our hypothesis, we analyzed publicly available genomic datasets in IMR-90 cells to examine the spatial arrange­ ment of genes encoding adhesome proteins and their regulators. When interrogating these Hi-C maps, we identified that the adhesome genes were spatially clustered, with transcriptionally active adhesome genes being co-clustered. We next tested whether genes encoding the transcriptional regulators of active adhesome genes were spatially adjacent to their target loci. Upon matrix sensing, various downstream signal processes are triggered including some of the adhesome proteins serving as transcription factors, cofactors, and chromatin regulators. We found that genes encoding many of these transcription regulators are co-localized within the adhesome gene clusters. Extending our analysis to identify ­non-adhesome genes that are co-localized within the adhesome gene clusters, we identified genes of the ubiquitin-proteasome system – a sys­ tem known to be involved in the regulation of focal adhesions [72]. In order to test if the adhesome gene clusters identified using population-level Hi-C maps are physically close-by in single cells, we took advantage of recent DNA-MERFISH data in IMR-90 cells, which includes probes associated with adhesome genes [30]. To provide additional validation, we labelled a subset of adhesome genes identified in our analysis along with control genes using DNA-FISH. We indeed find that the adhesome gene loci are spatially sub-clustered and show higher local phosphorylated RNA Pol2 signal. Together with the analysis of the MERFISH dataset, these experiments validate at the single-cell level that many of the adhesome genes and their transcriptional regulators are spatially clustered. We note, however, that the clustered organization of adhesome genes could also arise as a secondary consequence of transcriptional activity, for example, through local condensation of RNA Pol2 and associated factors. Although our analyses show increased transcription and RNA Pol2 occupancy at adhesome loci, our current data do not allow us to disentangle whether spatial gene clustering is a cause or a consequence of elevated tran­ scriptional activity. Collectively, our results highlight a link between protein clustering on the membrane and gene clustering in the cell nucleus. Typical matrix sensing involves the clustering of receptors in the first few minutes, followed by adhesome maturation and cellular responses in the next tens of minutes, which is then followed by cell behavioral responses in subse­ quent hours to days [73]. Whether similar spatial organization contributes to other receptor-mediated responses to microenvi­ ronmental signals remains an open question.
